title: The ladder of humility (Rule 7)
hookLine: twelve rungs, from fear of God to a humble love

cards: A man is running from his brother. Night comes.

He lies down in the open with a stone for a pillow, and he dreams: "behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it."
That's Jacob, in Genesis. Benedict reads that dream in chapter seven of his Rule, and sees in it the shape of a humble life. Up and down.
And he counts the rungs: twelve of them.

teach.h: DOWN BY PRIDE, UP BY HUMILITY.
teach.b: The chapter opens with a line from Jesus: "whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted." Then Benedict turns it into a picture.
On Jacob's ladder, he says, we go down by lifting ourselves up, and we go up by humbling ourselves.
The two side rails, he says, are our body and our soul, and God has set the rungs between them.
So what are the rungs? The bottom one is to keep the fear of God always before your eyes, never forgetting that God sees. From there they climb through things you can actually do.
Not insisting on your own way. Bearing hard things patiently, without walking off. Telling the abbot your hidden thoughts, instead of letting them fester.
Being content with the plain, low job. Speaking gently, and not too much. Not being quick to laugh.

And the top rung: a humility that shows even in how you walk and stand, quiet, unshowy. Then the payoff. When the monk has climbed all twelve, Benedict says, he'll come to the love of God that casts out fear.

He's borrowing John's letter: "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear." So the ladder starts with fear and ends with love. What began as effort, done out of fear, becomes habit, done out of love.
Humility here isn't only a feeling about yourself. It's a set of things you do: getting your own way out of the way, one rung at a time, until love is what's left.

how: Benedictine communities read chapter seven of the Rule aloud in turn with the rest, and the twelve steps are used as a way to examine everyday conduct: speech, patience, obedience and the willingness to take the lowest place.

games.q: you're Benedict, reading Jacob's dream of angels on a ladder. what do you see in it?
o: the way of humility: down by pride, up by humbling yourself.
a warning never to sleep outside.
games.why: Benedict reads the ladder as humility: by exalting ourselves we go down, by humbling ourselves we go up.

practice: Look at the rungs again: not insisting on your own way, bearing something hard without complaining, speaking gently and a little less, taking the plain job without a fuss.

One will feel like the one you need, so choose it for today and picture where you'll meet it: the meeting, the dishes, the person who always gets under your skin. If you pray, ask for help with that one rung.

wordCard.voice: The ladder of humility. Benedict's twelve rungs, climbed by humbling yourself, from the fear of God to a love that casts out fear.

orig.note: Latin, the word in the title of Rule chapter seven: humility.

carryVoice: Your line: humility is a ladder. Miss a rung, and it's still there tomorrow. See you tomorrow.
